body.text: Years ago, over curries at an embassy dinner, a charismatic Indian ambassador recounted some of his ripsnorting nicknames for fellow diplomats.
The Europeans, in particular the Scandinavians, he dubbed the “Axis of Good” because of smug human rights lectures delivered from high moral pedestals.

Those days might be numbered as European nations seek to borrow from Australia’s offshore immigration detention example and establish so-called return hubs in third countries for people with rejected asylum-seeker claims.

On Friday, Denmark hosted immigration ministers from Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece for talks, as a dozen demonstrators with megaphones and signs protested outside the Danish parliament.

“We expect to be ready to send the first foreigners to a partner country by the end of next year,” Danish immigration minister Morten Bødskov said, adding he hopes the first deal can be struck around New Year.
I felt moments of déjà vu as these European ministers parroted lines Australian politicians have used for decades.
The facilities will not be a prison or detention camp, he said.
“It is an agreement with a partner country that gives people that have no legal grounds to be here an opportunity to have a new chance in the partner country,” he said.
The five ministers will gather again in Munich later in September for further talks.
Fronting the media after the Copenhagen meeting, they had scant concrete details to share.

They insisted the return hubs “must have a measurable impact on reducing migration and perilous journeys to Europe” and that “Europe’s shared values and human rights must … be reflected in the way these arrangements are designed”.

As a former Canberra Press Gallery reporter who covered immigration at the height of Operation Sovereign Borders, I felt moments of déjà vu as these European ministers parroted lines Australian politicians have used for decades – “breaking the people smuggler’s business models” and “we will decide who comes to our country”.

It remains unclear exactly where duty of care or accountability on human rights violations would lie. The ministers said the International Organisation for Migration and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees would be involved in monitoring the centres.
Its Netherlands branch described the moves as “a shameless attempt by the EU to shirk its responsibilities regarding migration and shift them onto countries in the South”.
“(European) governments across the political spectrum are now dancing to the same xenophobic and racist tune,” Amnesty NL said.
Other European attempts to send asylum seekers to non-European Union countries have struggled.
The European Union has long considered itself a bastion of human rights and says the bloc’s work “remained grounded in our commitment to protect human rights and democracy”.

“No amount of chaos or conflict will ever change the fact that human dignity, justice and accountability are the only path to peace and prosperity for all,” the EU’s top diplomat said in the foreword of its 2025 human rights annual report.
